utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. I'll just quote from the transcript in the Krstic case and that is on page 2233, lines 19 to 22, and I'll -- you said the Muslim men because they said it was useless to them, so, which was confirmed, what you just mentioned, but then you added, "I then believed that they would go to Kladanj and that they would be escorted." So my question is simply, at that time, when this incident took place, or when this event took place, about the money that was useless to them, you had no reason to believe that these men would not be taken to Kladanj as all the people who were being taken to Kladanj at that time?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed the BSA story that they would be brought to Kladanj and that we could escort them. At that time, I was a Dutch soldier with the Geneva Conventions in the military education, of course, and I looked at that as being at a conflict between two western countries. I've never ever thought that the people that were inside that bus could have been killed by Bosnian Serbs at that time. I was -- I'd never had a conclusion that any army should do something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you had no reason to believe on what was going on that anything else was happening?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw was the separation of men from the families that were gathered around the UN headquarters. I saw the men taken into a "White House." The men were terrified. They wanted to convince me that they were killed. They offered me their money with -- which I didn't took. They made the signal from the right to the left shoulder. I informed them that they would be taken to Kladanj and that because I believed the either army, the BSA army at that time, because they said you will escort them and we will bring them to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's the basis or the assumptions on which you were operating?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I thought that they would be brought to Kladanj to get out of the bus because there were elder men and of course it wasn't -- later on you say, well, that was very naive.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, well, I will --

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will not have that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's your answer but that it stays there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, please, please. Colonel, you just answer the questions that are put to you and you address the Trial Chamber and not Mr. Bourgon directly. No across-the-table comments. Mr. Bourgon, the same applies to you. Proceed with your questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the Geneva Conventions and that you were trained on the Geneva Conventions but you were also a professional, professionally trained army officer and you would agree with me that it's normal to disarm the persons that you will either be detained or that will be interned, to disarm is a normal procedure?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when you consider them as prisoners of war, it is, but I don't know that these men were prisoners of war. They were elder men and younger boys, there were no --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If, let's take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him finish the answer. I'm not sure that he had finished the answer, Mr. Bourgon, his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So when you asked me about what will you do with hostile fighters or soldiers, you could have course take their weapons and detain them and interrogate them. That is what is in the Geneva Convention of course, but these group of people were elder men and younger boys. They didn't belong to an army or of a division.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I take your -- that might have been your observation that they did not belong to an army, but my question is straightforward. If you have fighting personnel or soldiers that you detain or that you intern it is normal to disarm them and to interrogate them, which is what you just said?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I suggest to you that one of the things that they were interested in knowing from these people is where all the armed men from the enclave had vanished.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I've never asked about the other men who vanished from the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And one last question because you mentioned the Geneva Conventions, that you know that the Geneva Conventions ask of you, that you keep separated the soldiers and civilians. You are aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the three buses on which you saw these persons loaded from the "White House," you mention in your testimony that they were -- you were told that they did not make it to Kladanj but you were told this information days later. That's according to your testimony. I just want to confirm that this is something that you were never able to confirm. It's something you heard days later.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you know, I was a guest of the BSA during the night that followed, and when I get back to the compound I spoke to the Lieutenant who was on the car which had to go all the way to Kladanj with the men and he told me that he was stopped nearby Bratunac with an AK 47 on his head and that they had to return. So that's the only thing I said and I can't add anything else to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We'll just go back to exactly what you said and that is on page 2234, line 17 to 22. And you said at that time, "I left with convoy number 4, later on, but some days later, I've been told, those three buses never left Bratunac. They went to Bratunac and the escort was stopped there by the Bosnian Serbs." So neither you nor the person who reported that information to you days later knows what happened with those three buses?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's correct, because when I had my convoy to Kladanj I couldn't return to the compound the same day, and I had to stay overnight so some days later it was told to me by this Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, on your way to Kladanj and I think that was during -- when you took the second convoy, you mention seeing BSA soldiers firing in into the woods. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen them firing inside -- towards the woods, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the Prosecution made a point of asking you if anyone in the woods returned fire, and your answer was no.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you would agree with me, as a professional military officer, that if there were indeed Muslims in the woods, of course if, then if they would fire back, they would reveal their position and draw fire upon them, and it's a good reason why they would not return fire.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or another reason is that they won't have any weapons at all to fire with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm just asking you that first possibility is one but the possibility I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a possibility as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, another possibility is that they are not there at all?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a third one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on the road, you also mentioned having seen vehicles with a giant wolf head. And that was testimony here on 18 of October, page 97, lines 10 to 12. And looking at what you said, you mention, "I guess it was the Drina Wolves." You remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I -- I saw was a wolf's head and of course I'm testified in the Krstic case and then it became clear that it could be a Drina Corps car that I've seen but at that time I only saw the wolf's head on the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So at that time, you did not see -- you did not know or have any information what that wolf's head meant in terms of what unit could have been present?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you did not know if the people or the soldiers around these vehicles had any relationship with the vehicle or the vehicles, because you said many vehicles, with the wolf's head; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I only saw blue camouflage uniforms and normal camouflage uniforms who were there in the nearance of the cars with the wolf's head.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I suggest to you that vehicles from the Drina Wolves do not have any wolf's head on them, is it possible you saw something else?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that if you tell me that the Drina Wolves don't have wolf's heads on their cars, I'm sure that you're right, but the only thing I saw was a wolf's head on the car, and I can't -- I can't add anything to -- towards that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the answer you just gave you say on the car because when you testified on -- when you responded to the questions of my colleague, you mention vehicles in plural. How many vehicles did you see with a wolf's head?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the number. It could have been two or one or three but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If in the Krstic case you answered only one vehicle, would that be the case?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that that was at least one. It could have been two but I don't recall that specifically right now, 11 years later, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, throughout the time you spent in -- in those events let's say from 5 July until 14th of July I would just like to confirm that you never met or encountered anyone from the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, sir, because I've seen BSA infantry. I don't know whether they belonged to the Zvornik Brigade. I've met a few lieutenants when I was at the school. I don't know which units they belonged to so I can't tell you that I've never met them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But my question is very precise. When you are in Potocari or when you are on the way with those convoys, or when you are in your blocking position, did you encounter anyone who introduced himself as a member of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a specific question, and nobody introduced himself to me as a member of the Zvornik Brigade but I don't know whether they were when I saw them nearby the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I agree with that but you never met anyone from the Zvornik Brigade during those events?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who was identifying himself as being a member of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I appreciate your answer. One last question I have for you is that there is a distinct difference between the weapons used by the UN, which is the FN, and the weapons used by the parties, which is the AK 47. It's very easy to distinguish the two for someone who was in July 1995 --

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions. Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. I think we can take the break now. We will reconvene in 25 minutes' time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's you, Mr. Lazarevic, who goes next.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic will be cross-examining you now, and he appears for Accused Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Egbers. With your assistance this will be a very brief examination. I just wish to clarify certain points of your testimony you gave over the previous two days. During your testimony on the 18th of October 2006 you said that you spent the night between the 11th and the 12th of July 1995 at the UN base in Potocari. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, telling you that. Is it in the line?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, that was the night on the 11th, when you came to the Potocari base and you spent the night there. That's the part of your testimony I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's correct but I'm not that strong in all those dates from the days so I was two days at blocking position 1 and I went back to Potocari before I had a tour with the buses, so I was there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I didn't think that this detail was going to be unknown to you but that was the night before you went with the convoy and the buses. That's your testimony on the 18th of October, page 93 to 94. You said that after you spent the night there, you awoke and your task was to escort the buses and that by that time, the buses had already arrived at the UN base in Potocari. Do you recall that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that part of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this particular point, could you be as precise as possible and estimate the time you awoke, as far as you can?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I awoke early in the morning but I don't know the exact time. It was before the buses entered the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You seem to have anticipated my next question. Therefore, the buses arrived after you woke up?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Another question in connection with this: Had the evacuation already started at the point you were given the order to escort the convoy?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It didn't start until we, with two vehicles, could accompany the buses towards Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I conclude on the basis of your answer that you escorted the first convoy, or rather that there was no other convoy leaving for Kladanj before the one you escorted.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my recollection, that I had to escort the first convoy. I don't know whether others might have left the enclave with buses which I didn't see but I can only tell you what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us at what time approximately the convoy set off?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Another question on this particular point: In that first convoy you accompanied, were there any men?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've only seen women and children in the first convoy. I haven't seen any elder or younger men at that time, and as I told you, I had to drive behind the last bus, the bus broke down, and I focused on that bus and there were no men on that bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you a document now. This is your debriefing dated 11 September 1995. That is Exhibit 2D25. Can we please take a look at page 11, paragraph 3, in the English version? You see paragraph 3, line first of your debriefing. It says there were mainly women and children in the buses. Now, on the basis of what you stated here, in particular that you used the term "mainly," does it mean that there were men after all in the convoy, as you would have remembered that much better at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't anything -- I can't add anything. I can't exclude that there were men as well. There were mainly women and children, and in the bus that broke down there were only women and children inside the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I understand your answer to mean that you cannot exclude the possibility that there were men on the buses, is that a fair interpretation of your answer?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't exclude it but I haven't seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On the 12th, when the convoy set off for Bratunac, you had to pass by OP Papa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th, were there DutchBat members at OP Papa still there at the time?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your trip from Potocari to Kladanj, you explained that the bus broke down and you explained the circumstances in which you carried on with your trip. Can you tell us at what time the bus broke down, either in hours or in terms of the relationship in time from the time you set off?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only 30 minutes after we left. We passed Bratunac and then turned left, and there it broke down. I showed it on the map yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This happened approximately near the village of Glogova; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen the village but it was on the road, and I have added on the map, I think a big -- I've underlined it yesterday, so I didn't say that it was nearby the village but it was in the nearance of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That is not of the greatest relevance. I'd like to know how long you spent there at the roadside from the point the bus broke down to the point when the refugees boarded the bus.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was -- the bus broke down and it took 45 minutes to an hour to get a new bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Once you resumed your trip, did you at some point join the convoy that was on its way to Kladanj and with which you had initially set off?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I joined the convoy at Kladanj, so there were buses and I arrived there with the last bus of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as you can, can you tell us when did you travel the section of the road from Glogova to Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was I think ten minutes after we -- or 15 minutes after we left but I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As you arrived at your destination in the vicinity of Kladanj, you informed OP Alpha that the convoy had passed through; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived -- when I reached Kladanj, I radioed that I was at Kladanj and that all the buses were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can you tell us exactly when did you pass that section of the road between Glogova and Konjevic Polje? Was it in the morning hours, in the afternoon hours, was it early morning, late morning? Could you be specific?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that day, I first met General Mladic. Then the buses were ready to go. So we left at the beginning of the -- I think it was in the beginning of the evening. We had an hour delay so it was at that time -- I'm not sure about the times but it was in the afternoon that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Could we move on to the following day, the 13th of July, 1995? You testified that you accompanied the convoy from Potocari to Kladanj on that day as well. Do you recall that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The convoy you accompanied on the 13th, was it the first convoy to leave on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that. I can't recall it. We have numbered the convoys but I'm not sure whether convoy 1 left that day. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. But can you tell us at least when the convoy you escorted on the 13th set off, at what time?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the morning, but it wasn't in the beginning of the morning. It was -- because I first witnessed the separation of the men and women. That convoy left, then there was the men going into the buses, and then it was me. So there must be convoys during that morning and I think at the end of the morning, I left with my convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I understand your answer correctly, you stated that there were convoys leaving ahead of you and that in these convoys, men were separated from women. Is that the gist of your answer?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning, I saw men being separated from their families. They were inside buses. I don't know whether it was convoy number 3 or convoy number 4, but one of the two was convoy with the men and the other one with the women and children. They were escorted by my vehicle. So I can't exclude that there were more convoys leaving that morning but I'm not sure about that. I can't tell you with 100 per cent certainty that it happened that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. As you arrived to your destination near Kladanj with that second convoy, did you inform OP Alpha of your arrival there?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you travelled with the other convoy on the 13th, you also passed by OP Papa and did you see any DutchBat members there at the time?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that. I followed the buses. That was where I was focusing on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Finally, I'd like to move to some events you described in your evidence, and which have to do with "White House." At page 21 of the transcript during your yesterday's testimony, you said that you went to the "White House" because you heard a woman screaming because her husband had been separated from her and had been taken in the direction of the "White House." You also stated that you entered the "White House" and that you saw men seated in all the rooms waiting to see what would become of them and that you spoke to them briefly. That's the gist of your yesterday's evidence. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us more specifically now at what time or what time of day it was when you went to the "White House"?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the morning, before my convoy left. So I don't know the exact time but it was in the early -- in the morning, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a part of your statement to the OTP investigators, given to them on the 24th of October 1995. That is Exhibit 2D19. Before I ask you some matters about this statement, you were able to see this statement of yours yesterday but at the time you were giving this statement, did you give it to the best of your recollection and knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you ask me questions about my testimony yesterday or what was written down?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the statement you gave to the OTP investigators on the 24th of October 1995.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that was an interview so they asked me questions and they wrote the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question is whether your asked answers were to the best of your recollection and knowledge at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you this as well, in 1995 in the month of October, three months after the relevant events, your memory was much fresher than it is today, many years later?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the problem with witness statements in 1995 were that it wasn't -- it was an interview and it was reported by the Dutch government, so it was an interview during the day and the things they thought were relevant were typed out. So when you ask me specific questions about the colour of his eyes or the colour of his hair, it didn't seem that important in 1995, so when you ask me questions about what happened at that time of day, it could be that it's not in the original witness statement because I wasn't asked of it, and she interpreted it and she wrote it down and that's what we discussed. So it's -- of course, this is what I could remember then but when the investigators didn't ask me the questions, I couldn't answer them as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a very simple question which you could have answered with a yes or a no. The suggestion is to you to accept that way back in 1995, in the month of October, three months after the events when you were then interviewed, your memory would have been much fresher, much better, or fresher or better than it is today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Finally, can we see page 5, paragraph 2 of your statement dated the 24th of October 1995? Did you see the part starting with the words, "I went in" and I will read it for you. It says here, "[In English] I went in and I saw a Muslim man sitting on the first room on the right-hand side after the entrance. He was sitting alone. The other rooms on the ground floor were empty. I did not go upstairs." [Interpretation] These are your words describing the events in the "White House" in 1995. Therefore, you entered the house, you saw a man seated in one room, whereas all the other rooms on the ground floor were empty and you didn't go upstairs. My question to you is: Do you stand by this statement of yours that you gave back in 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I can recall it, I went upstairs and I spoke to other men and they -- so it's not correct in this statement. I went upstairs, and I had a look, and I spoke to these men as well as I spoke to them when they went into the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you wish to say that your 1995 statement is not correct in this part?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I can remember it right now, it's not correct for me not going upstairs because I can remember that, that I've been there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I just intervene here and ask a question: On that day, the 13th of July, did you enter into one house only or possibly more than one house in the vicinity of the compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was just one house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One house. Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. I understood next one is to be Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Change of plan again, Your Honour. Mr. Krgovic negotiates these things on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau. Madam Fauveau is representing General Miletic on these things and she will be cross-examining you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, before you left for Srebrenica or when you arrived at Srebrenica, were you briefed as to the task of the DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Wasn't one of the tasks to demilitarise the enclave?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that the enclave was never demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we entered the enclave there was a weapon collection point and all the weapons should have been into the weapon collection point, but there were men carrying weapons inside the enclave. That's what I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we say that at the time when you left for Srebrenica, it never came up as an issue to defend the enclave?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not there to defend the enclave. Well, the only thing we had to do was to report things we saw at the observation post. There was no force, there was no force, Dutch force, inside the enclave that could defend such a terrain.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Indeed, you did not have the means to defend the enclave but you had enough means to carry out your task, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell you about my own task, as a platoon leader, and I had a platoon with one observation post, we could manage. The only thing we did was patrolling the area during the day, and we weren't even in the area during the night so we could never defend it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: My question was with regard to your ordinary tasks, the one that were part of your mission to the enclave. Did you have enough means for that?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I look at my own means, an entire platoon with 30 men, and APCs, that could manage the observation post. But when -- there was a lot of pressure on the ammunition, for instance. We had no fresh ammunition. We had no food delivered. We had no diesel delivered. So if you ask me whether we could ever -- we could carry out our mission, it was no, because we couldn't get stuff inside it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 2D25?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could I take you to page 5? Paragraph with the heading, "Logistics." Sir, this is one of your prior statements to the Dutch authorities. On that occasion, this is what you stated. "[In English] There was sufficient equipment to be available to be able to protect himself but not to defend the enclave. It was not their assignment to defend the enclave. His impression was that they were given sufficient resources to be able to function in the enclave."

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the situation when we entered the enclave. We had enough diesel to use the cars we had but as you know, people from my platoon were -- had a permission to leave the enclave to go for a short break to Zagreb, but never had the permission to go back to the enclave to join the platoon again.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you agree that nothing in this statement you have in front of you is limited to the very beginning of your time of service in the enclave? There is no date attached to this paragraph, is there?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. So I just explained it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Today you testified about two Englishmen belonging to the SAS. Could you tell us what their task was?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were with our Special Forces in the enclave, and I have had them on OP -- on Bravo 1 and they had radio contact with other UN troops. I don't know which troops they were. But there were two SAS NCOs in the enclave. I don't know what specific their task was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know when they arrived in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were there I thought in January as well, so I've seen them for a long time, for several months.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Were they under the command of Lieutenant Colonel Karremans or were they under another command?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. They were no member of my platoon or my company. They were seated with the other Special Forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Earlier on you mentioned the permission for transportation that were not given to DutchBat members or rather that they were not authorised to return into the enclave. Do you know who would grant such authorisations?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I can recall, it was the Bosnian Serb army that would -- granted us to get the men and the equipment back into the enclave. That's what -- that was told to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know which was the organ in charge of these permissions or authorisations?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. The only thing I know is that it was told by my company commander that one of our generals had to speak about that with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I suppose that when you mentioned commands, you meant Lieutenant Colonel Karremans?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed by my company commander, Matthijssen and of course he's in the line. He is one of the commanders of -- he's under the command of Karremans so I didn't talk to Mr. Karremans myself. I was talked about this -- I talked about this with my company commander who told me that generals would speak about this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, were you taken hostage by the Muslims whilst you were in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, at the Bandera Triangle in the west of the enclave, as we entered the enclave in January 1995. Could have been February as well. In the winter.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the conditions of detention were rather bad?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stayed in our vehicle at -- during two nights. And it was cold outside, as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the men who took you hostage were under the command of a man named Zulfo?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what they told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The Muslim forces under the command of Zulfo, were they in charge of the area between OPA and OPC?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they told me, that Zulfo was in charge of men who were in that side of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can it be said that these Muslim forces commanded by Zulfo were well organised?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- I can't say that because they were blocking us on the road. They communicated with notes. I've never seen Mr. -- this Mr. Zulfo. So the negotiations went on a higher level, with -- by this commander of DutchBat. So I don't know whether they were organised well or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown the same exhibit, 2D25, but we'd like to turn to page 6. Second paragraph, please. There is a sentence in the middle of the paragraph, "[In English] The area around OPA was never calm during the entire period. Zulfo was the leader of the Muslims between OPC and OPA. The Muslims in this area were well organised." [Interpretation] Sir, would you agree that the Muslims were well organised in this area?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were better organised in this area than the other area of the enclave, because Zulfo was a man they were all afraid of, and he -- what he told had to be done, well, it was done. So they were better organised but you can't compare this to an army organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that after this incident when you were taken hostage, the UNPROFOR forces could no longer get into the area called the Bandera Triangle?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a piece of landscape belonging to the southern part of the enclave. It was under the command of the Bravo Company so I don't know whether they were able to go into observation post Charlie again. I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can I refresh your memory? We are still dealing with Exhibit 2D25, this time page 4. First paragraph. Last sentence. "[In English] After a while, the UNPROFOR was no longer allowed to enter the so-called Bandera Triangle. It was unclear why."

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, do you remember that the UNPROFOR was no longer allowed to enter the Bandera Triangle area?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a problem when we came in, we had this blockation of the roads for a few days, but I'm not -- I didn't get in the triangle but I had nothing to do there so those questions has to be answered by the Bravo Company who was there. I don't know whether they went in at any time. I can't recall that. But whether it was allowed or not, during that time, they said, well, we are -- we are here in this triangle.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the 18th of October 2006, page 83 of the transcript, you said that you also belonged to a reserve battalion. When you were part of the reserve battalion, were you under the command of Captain Groen?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether I've used the word battalion but that's not the correct word. There was a reserve force, and it only had four APCs and each APC had a driver, a gunner, and a commander. So that was the reserve. A reserve battalion, it never was, of course, and I was under the command of Captain Groen at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown P2263?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is an order dated the 9th of July 1995, sent by Major Franken to Captain Groen. Through this order, as can be seen in the first paragraph, DutchBat were ordered to prevent the BSA from entering the town and towards the end of the paragraph, we see that this is a green order or assignment. Were you able to read this first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am. I see this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Well, you anticipated my question. I was about to ask you that. So you never saw this order before?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that when you were on position B 1, Bravo 1, you were next to a piece of Muslim artillery?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And was it the first time that you became aware that the Muslim forces in the enclave had artillery?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did the army of Republika Srpska bomb the positions that were around you?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that you never thought that the BSA was bombing your position?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, they were -- I wasn't sure about that but the second time, when I drove to another position, I was shelled there as well. So then that's when I reported that they were shelling us.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we show the witness Exhibit 5D77, please? I need the end of the first page right now, and then at the beginning of the second page. This is a report by NIOD, and the last sentence on the last page says as follows: "[In English] Even though Lieutenant Egbers was shot by the VRS he did not believe that the VRS deliberately shot at DutchBat." [Interpretation] So now if we look at page 6, we need to see the footnotes, please, footnote number 3. You see that footnote number 3 which is where the excerpt I read comes from, is excerpted from an interview with you that we don't have. But could you tell us whether this sentence in the NIOD actually states what you said in that interview that you gave in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I just declared, we were shelled several times, and I've described the first shelling, that I wasn't 100 per cent sure that they were shelling me because of the piece of artillery just in the neighbourhood, and it wasn't -- it was mortar fire so you can't aim at a specific target at that time. So when the first shells fell, I could not report to Captain Groen that it was aimed at my position because of the other position of the Muslim fighters. But later on I got shelled again, and when I drove away from the position, the shelling continued. So that was clear to me that I was shelled at that time by the Bosnian Serb army, but in the first time I wasn't sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to page 1 of this document, please. And ask the witness to carefully read the last paragraph on that page.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree with me if you say -- if I say that this paragraph does not relate to a specific shelling but just to a general situation?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this says something about the smoking gun and there was close air support so, the close air support was on my position so I ordered -- I informed my commander, Captain Groen, at that time, that I was shelled and that's why the two Dutch F-16s were sent in to help me. So at first, so your question was clear. This is generally spoken but as a result of the shelling of my position, and even when I drove away with the vehicles, the shelling continued, the close air support was called in.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You also said that when you were in that blocking position, you could see the BSA entering in villages and burn houses, is that true?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw from that blocking position was the village of Pusmulici and there what I saw together with my soldiers via a binocular that there was BSA coming into those houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You did not see the fire in the houses?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the smoke coming out of the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If there had been combat in that village, would you have seen the combat?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. How can I answer this question? I only saw the smoke. I saw the men coming -- going into the houses. I haven't seen the fighting but I can't tell you whether I should have seen the fighting if it was there. I don't know whether it was there or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness Exhibit 5D78? To save time it's another report by NIOD. It's another extract by NIOD. We need page 3, last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at the sentence starting by DutchBat? It says on the fourth line, and this is what it says: "[In English] [Microphone not activated] [Microphone not activated]?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that Madam Fauveau is reading in English but we are not -- was it just your microphone that wasn't on? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The transcript says "[Microphone not activated]."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I just Madam Fauveau that you start reading again, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: "DutchBat could see the Bosnian Serbs advance with tanks and their forces clear out the villages. The VRS systematically torched all houses scattered along the road possibly because ABiH soldiers that were still putting up a defence had converted the houses into defensive positions."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is a question I'd like to ask. What you saw from your position, could that correspond to the description I just read to you?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I haven't seen any fighting along those houses. The only thing I saw was the smoke coming out of the houses, and the BSA entering the enclave at Pusmulici so these are conclusions but I can't draw those conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And if there had been snipers in that house, could you have seen them work?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were snipers in houses. I don't know whether I could have seen them. These are all questions -- I haven't seen them, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said today at page 18 that you saw the Muslims, in July 85 [as interpreted] in -- weapons only in July. So before that date, when you saw men with weapons, you were supposed to take their weapons away, right? 24

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So wouldn't it be logical to deduct that the Muslims hid their weapons whenever they saw UN forces?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can say is that I haven't seen them on -- until that summer. So when you ask me whether it should be logical or not, I think it would be logical but I don't know where you want to go to with these questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So during that period in July 1995, right before the collapse of the enclave, when you saw the Muslim and civilian Muslims with weapons, is it fair to say that it was really difficult to make a difference between the military men and civilian men? Talked about able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I saw Muslim men carrying weapons, and you're asking me whether it's difficult to tell you the difference between a soldier and a non-combatant. I think -- are you aiming at that? Because I don't understand the question, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I want to know. Making a difference between a civilian and military people, when it comes to able-bodied men. Is it difficult to make?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you left the blocking post and arrived in Srebrenica, you said earlier today that you saw military people on the marketplace in Srebrenica. I would like now to show you a short video. It's the P2047, and it's a 1 minute 30 long sequence starting at 4.45.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, does this correspond to what you saw in Srebrenica when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you ask me whether I recognise the environment or the roads or --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the gas station. It must be the same gas station as is in the south of the UN base of the Bravo Company.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that if I say that the only explosion that we can hear in this video had to come from Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So from a military point of view, would it be logical for the VRS to respond to this explosion?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can answer the question because it is just a piece of mortar that fired. I don't know the circumstances we are in. I don't know whether it's fore [phoen] or not. I don't have any other information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But you recognise the place from where that shot was fired?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you confirm that this place was very close to where all the refugees were, all the women, the children and the elderly?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see all the refugees on the video. So I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we now show the witness Exhibit 5D79? Page 5, please. And the middle paragraph that starts with"Honing" [phoen]. It's the description of an event made by one of your colleagues in the DutchBat. "[In English] You saw with my own eyes how someone within the crowd just outside our fence fired off a small mortar in the direction of the Bosnian Serb positions. I saw the smoke from the shot. That Muslim soldiers hid behind the women and children. What a disgrace for a soldier. That kind of incident didn't do much to increase our respect for the Muslim army." [Interpretation] Does this description correspond to what we saw on the video?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so because there is no Dutch APC on the video as well, and I don't know whether it was a Dutch video.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But the party -- the fact that they were hiding behind women and children, could that apply to this incident also?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, because I saw a mortar fire, you don't have to fire a mortar in front of the other troops. The mortar will fire a few thousand metres away. So I can't connect this video to this statement. I'm sorry, you have to ask this Mr. Honing belonging to the Bravo Company. I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show the witness the Exhibit 5D81? Page 2, the paragraph before last.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So according to what we read in this paragraph, "[In English] Probably at that point near the market square that the DutchBat soldier used his weapon. The said soldier was guarding the rear of one of the APCs when he saw a man emerging from behind the house and climb up his weapon to shoot at the APC. The DutchBat soldier thinking it was an antitank weapon fired and hit the potential assailant who fell to the ground. The APC immediately drove away." [Interpretation] Do you have any knowledge of this event?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I read it?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, of course. Oui.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it. Your question was, Madam?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have any knowledge of this incident?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You're talking today about the evacuation of the Srebrenica people, and you agree to say that it was the UN that initiated the evacuation in the first place. I would like now to show you a short video, 20 seconds long, P2045.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I don't believe, in fact -- if that was a question, I don't believe that that was in fact what the witness has agreed to or has said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say that the UN initiated the deportation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There was one question that was asked by Mr. Bourgon this morning that Madam Fauveau is referring to, yes, and I think the witness in a way did accept that proposition, that the first movement of refugees was as a result of action taken by -- but we can go straight to the page. Which page is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We are talking, Mr. President, from Srebrenica to Potocari, just to make it clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's another kind of evacuation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So which line? So the question by Mr. Bourgon was the following: "I'd like to address the way between Srebrenica and Potocari, when the population started to move along with yourself and a couple of DutchBat vehicles. If I suggest to you that this movement towards Potocari was actually initiated by the UN because the population was panicking and did not know what would that be," and it stops there. The witness's answer was that it would be correct, we tried to get them out of Potocari, of Srebrenica, towards Potocari. That's the question and the answer as it shows in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I thought she was referring to the deportation of the women and children from Potocari to Kladanj, but that's my mistake, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me read the question again. I think it was your mistake because I think it's clear enough, because she was obviously referring you to your previous part of the testimony, which couldn't but have been to the evacuation from Srebrenica in the direction of Potocari. So let's repeat the question, Madam Fauveau, please, and then he can proceed with the answer. Actually, there is no question. You're going to show him the video, which is P2045? And we can take it up from there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's sequence starting at 13.20.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, are these the images that you saw in Srebrenica on July 11th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there at that time, and I saw things like this happen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you agree to say that the UN vehicle transporting these people were overloaded?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: With your own vehicle, you evacuated people from the Srebrenica hospital. Is it fair to say that the people that you evacuated were sick people and you did not see any wounded among them?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had sick people. I don't recall whether there were wounded inside of the hospital but we evacuated the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree with me to say that you did not know whether there were any wounded, you did not see them with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in Bravo 1, at the blocking position, I saw a Muslim man wounded at the stomach. But I don't know what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: That man you're talking about who was at the blocking position, was a Muslim soldier fighting against the BSA, right?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a Muslim standing nearby a piece of artillery that wasn't used.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, on October 18, in that statement at page 93, you said that when you came to Potocari with the refugees there were no water for the refugees. I'd like now to show you Exhibit 5D67. This is the last part of paragraph 1, please. This is what it says. No. It's the last part of paragraph 2, sorry. This is what it says. [In English] "Info received indicates that BSA have accepted to assist with food and water." [Interpretation] Do you know that two water tanks arrived in Potocari? Do you know of that?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there when they got -- if they got there. I haven't seen them. The only thing I saw was a UN water facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now that you have this document in front of your eyes, in paragraph 3, do you see, "[In English] With regard to the fuel situation in the enclave, MSF have 800 litres, UNHCR 6.000 litres." [Interpretation] Do you know that the UNHCR had fuel?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show the witness now 1D35, please. Can we turn to page 2, please? It was the end of the fourth paragraph which is the first paragraph on this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Please, can you read this. "[In English] Potocari has not been cut by the Serbs and thus water is available for the people." For your information this is a document sent by Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan on the 12th of July 1995. Does this remind you of the fact that there was water in the Potocari compound?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there a question for me?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're being invited to accept the proposition that there was water in Potocari, there was no short -- in the compound, that there was no shortage of it, in other words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the only thing I see are reports that I've seen for the first time. The only thing I know is that we had water in cans and we were able to make fresh water from the water which was in the rivers, and that it took a lot of diesel and a lots of time to make clear drinkable water for us. That's the only thing I know. I don't know whether there was BSA support by giving water to the refugees. I haven't seen that. The only thing I saw was that we were running out of our own water that was in cans and could be made of water just in the river, but as I stated, that was my condition at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you testified about the "White House." Is it fair to say that all you said about the "White House" happened on the 13th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same day that I left with my convoy and didn't return after the night with the Bosnian Serbs. If that is the 13th, then it's the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can it be said that on the 12th of July 1995, you didn't see anybody in the "White House"?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of that because I was escorting the first convoy, and there was General Mladic with us, he had some bread, photographs and press with him. So the first convoy was going as planned and with normal groups of women and children inside the buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more time do you require, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should be finished by the break, another three or four questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Krgovic and Mr. Haynes, you will have left 45 hours between you. Do you think you would be able -- 45 minutes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I would hope to complete my entire cross-examination for the case in 45 hours but we will do our best to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, I appeal to you to do that. I don't know if there is re-examination. Not at this moment, I see. Let's proceed, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes. You personally, and I'm only asking you about what you were able to see on the 12th of July, you did not witness the separation of the men from the women, did you?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, in the morning of that day, when Major Franken warned you that you would have to leave with the convoy, you stated on the 18th of October that in fact Major Franken wanted to put one man into each bus but that had not been allowed by the Serbs. That is what you testified on page 94 on the 18th of October. Do you remember this statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Isn't it fair to say that indeed DutchBat did not have enough men to place one soldier on board each and every bus?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of DutchBat troops who didn't have a fighting assignment. There were cooks, there were mechanics and I don't know how many soldiers we had left but there were a lot of them inside the enclave but they were not the fighting infantry soldiers. So technically, it could have been happened of course when 12 buses drive all the way to Kladanj and go back again.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Were you present when one of the members of the Dutch -- of the Serbian authorities told Major Franken that he could not -- he was not allowed to put one man into each bus?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When Major Franken informed you of your task, that is that you were going to escort the convoys, you testified that the evacuation had not yet started but isn't it fair to say that the buses had not yet arrived in Potocari at that time?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can say is that I had to go to Major Franken and that he asked me to get ready, and I don't know whether he said that a few hours before or when the buses exactly arrived at the enclave, but we were surprised that there were buses coming into the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown Exhibit 2D24? Page 2, please. The paragraph starting with the words, "12th of July 1995."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, would you mind reading this, "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... 12 men in the conference hall who might be needed to escort the transports of refugees. Maletic, I think it was Mladic, was in the district at this time with a film crew. Then buses suddenly arrived and there was not really any time to negotiate." [Interpretation] Sir, would you agree that the buses arrived after Major Franken informed you of your task to accompany the buses?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it said.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you spoke with Major Franken on that morning, did he give you the order to assist in the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He ordered me to follow the bus and to let headquarters of DutchBat know where the buses went to because they didn't have any control of the route the buses were taken. So that's the only thing I can say, we had to follow the bus, and radio contact the observation post telling where the buses went.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown Exhibit 2D19? This is the statement made to the OTP on the 24th of October 1995. Page 4, third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, can you see this first sentence in paragraph 3, "[In English] I received the order to help evacuate the refugees."

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you allow for the fact that you might have received that order on the 12th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't helping the evacuation or deportation. I was ordered to report where they were going to so I didn't help them getting into the buses, I didn't help them to get a new bus. The only thing I did was to make sure that those women and children inside the buses went to a destination where they could go to Bosnian Muslim area so I didn't help the Bosnian Serb army with the evacuation. So it wasn't written down properly, in order that to help them getting into the bus or to show them the way where they had to go to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You escorted a first convoy which did arrive at its destination and the people left the buses there, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that you stayed there for an hour or so?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: During this one hour you spent there, did you see Major Boering leave with the Muslim refugees?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He left already, because I had this bus with the engine trouble, and I -- when I got there, the first women and children were walking their way to a Muslim area.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you arrived at your destination, were there some Serbian -- Serb soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the Serbian soldier does not mistreat anybody, did they?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't witnessed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir. No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. We'll have a 25-minute break, and then after that, hopefully we will be able to finish with your testimony today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You're now going to be examined by Mr. Josse who is representing General Gvero. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've already told us that were you were commander of 3rd Platoon of Charlie Company. I want to ask you whether you were aware at any time in 1995 of a crew from Charlie Company having been attacked by Muslim forces at -- overwhelmed by them and having their weapons taken.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? Is there a date?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I can. I get this for your information from something that Mr. Franken in fact mentioned. I suspect it was hearsay inasmuch as he had no firsthand knowledge of it but anyone who is interested it's page 2585 of the transcript. And I don't think he gave a specific date when he was asked about it. So I can't help any more than that, I'm afraid. Do you have any knowledge of it, as a platoon commander within Charlie Company?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Fine. Next point I'd like to ask you about is, you were shown a video earlier today of a mortar being fired from a disused petrol station in Srebrenica. I want to ask you about that -- that video depicts events on the 10th of July. You were there on the 11th of July. I'm right in saying that men of fighting age assembled in the vicinity of the Srebrenica petrol station on that day, the 11th of July, after which they departed in a northwesterly direction. Do you have any recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that day, at that time, I wasn't there nearby the gas station. So is the question for me that I -- if I have witnessed this?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't witnessed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you D225, please, which is your debriefing notes of the 11th of September of 1995, page 10. We can see the third paragraph down, "In the meantime, the men of fighting age were assembling in the vicinity of Srebrenica petrol station." That suggests, Lieutenant Colonel, and I put it no more highly than that, that you actually witnessed that happening, does it not?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw at that time was women, children and also men who were there but I haven't actually -- when you have me have a look at the video, there is -- is there a connection between the video and your question, because that's what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, only inasmuch as I wanted to make sure we are talking about the same place, namely the petrol station. Perhaps another way of locating this petrol station is that it was very near Bravo Company?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the connection. Let me make it clear, lest you or anyone else think I'm trying to confuse you, the video I understand was taken on the 10th of July. The event that I have referred you to in your debriefing notes are the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Any comment?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only thing I can say is that I was at the front of the refugees going from Potocari -- excuse me, from Srebrenica to Potocari, and all the vehicles that were left behind on the command of Captain Hageman. They stayed there and they tried to follow the last refugees to the north. So when there is any men who are meeting each other nearby the petrol station, it's not what I've seen happening but what others told me that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, were you personally in the Srebrenica hospital?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How far is the hospital from the petrol station?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It is in the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you ever visit the hospital at any stage?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You therefore have no firsthand knowledge as to what happened to the petrol -- to the hospital on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that I can declare about that is that people working for Medecins Sans Frontieres, I don't know there is an English word for that, they were asking me whether I could take the ill and wounded people from the hospital on the APC towards Potocari. They brought them to me and I drove with them to the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you receive any information as to any attack of any sort on the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to look it up. Not that I can recall right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't want to be unfair. Look it up where?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the statement you're presenting to me. Did you find it in my statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I haven't but I'm not suggesting that it may not be there.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. So I don't recall that at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. I'll come back to that in one moment's time because I have one or two other questions I want to ask you about the wounded in general. But before I do that, could I just ask you about another thing that you may have heard rather than seen? Did you hear a rumour on the 14th of July or thereabouts that some refugees had died in the compound at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I heard was that they were buried there on the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And from whom did that information come?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you said, that was the story that was going on. I haven't seen the graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It related, did it not, to six refugees, the rumour?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the number, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have a look, please, at D224. I may have got the numbering wrong here, in which case I'm going to deal with this differently because I want to move on. I have an undated debriefing of yours in which you had said, quote -- that is the right document. Page 4, please. About a third of the way down, it says, "He heard that six refugees had died at the compound. These dead refugees may have been buried in the vicinity of the compound." So that basically is what you've just told us, isn't it, that you do make reference to the number 6 there?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
